title: Improved Lithium-Ion Battery Cathode Cycling Stability at Higher Cut-Off Potential Using a Novel and Scalable Dual Coating Method
abstract: The electrification of transportation and the need for grid energy storage to accompany renewable energy require secondary batteries with higher energy density, longer useful lifespans and lower cost. In order for lithium-ion batteries, the most developed battery technology suitable for these uses, to achieve greater energy density at the cell level, the operating voltage window tolerated over the course of long-term cycling must be increased. In this work we have demonstrated a promising dual coating system of Li 2 SrSiO 4 and Al 2 O 3 achieved via an easily scalable sol gel technique and confirmed via XRD, used on commercial LiCoO 2 cathode powder. We demonstrate our finding that the optimal thickness of each coating can lead to increased specific capacity (~185 mAh/g at 0.5C) at a cut-off potential of 4.5 V and greater stability through multiple cycles at very high C rates (up to 10 C). Cyclic voltammetry was used to demonstrate reduced polarization, and therefore increased stability, after cycling in the dual coated cathodes relative to bare or Al 2 O 3 coated material. Fluorescence mapping of elemental distribution provides evidence of mechanical property advantages of the dual coating system, and the ability of the dual coating to preserve the cathode particles despite inhomogeneous thickness. The mechanism of the superior performance relative to bare and Al 2 O 3 coated cathodes was studied using scanning and transmission electron microscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and synchrotron X-ray spectroscopy in pristine and cycled cathodes. These findings have implications for the search for still better materials for which our simple coating method could be utilized. Additionally, we aim to gain insights into the transferable nature of the mechanisms by which this coating stabilizes cathodes at high voltage between the LiCoO2 utilized in this work, and experimental, lower cobalt cathode materials such as NMC811 or lithium-excess materials.

title: The Role of Cryogenic Treatment on the Properties of Various Metals and Polymers
abstract: Cryogenic treatment of materials is used to improve and strengthen the structure, grain, and elasticity of materials including ceramics, polymers, and metals. Process and material type used can influence the improvement of material properties that undergo cryogenic treatments, and can be performed in adjunction to heat treatment, quenching, and cold work [1]. The material properties may be improved including but not limited to hardness, wear resistance, material fatigue, and conductivity including superconductivity. Improvement in machining tools to increase the lifetime of work, stainless steel was one of the first materials to undergo cryogenic treatment [1]. Other metals and materials including brass, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, nylon, and plastics have been tested and treated to understand how cryogenic treatment changes the material structure and conductivity. Cryogenic treatment is used in a variety of treatments for metals and plastics that are used in different operations. Recent research has made discoveries in tool machining and material integrity as well as the behavior of materials strength and conductivity. Four research papers were reviewed to understand how cryogenic metal and polymer treatments are being used to strengthen and change material structure for prevention of fatigue. Metal machining is conducted at high temperatures, which decreases tool life. The cryogenic treatment of titanium alloys was investigated through thermal analysis of cutting temperature, tool wear, cutting operations, and dry machining [3,4]. Surface integrity of the titanium and machining performance was also used to determine that cryogenic treatment improved machining performance and tool wear [3]. title: Artificial Photosynthesis: Photoelectrochemical Water Splitting Using Cu 2 o
abstract: Photosynthesis is a biological process that converts energy from sunlight into chemical energy as an organic fuel. Cuprous oxide (Cu 2 O), a p-type semiconductor, was used to mimic this process as a cathode material for a photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting reaction. Cu 2 O can absorb energy from sunlight and convert it into a chemical form as hydrogen. The produced hydrogen can then be used as a clean fuel in devices like hydrogen fuel cells or further converted to ammonia (NH 3 ) for transport. In this study, thin layers of Cu 2 O crystals were deposited on a planar Cu substrate using chronoamperometry (CA) and characterized using scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Mott-Schottky analysis. The peak current density for the water splitting reaction was measured in a PEC cell using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV). The effect of deposition time was investigated as the Cu 2 O layer thickness has shown to affect the activity. The Cu 2 O prepared using a 5-minute deposition time showed the best performance relative to deposition times of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 minutes. The 5-minute deposition sample produced the highest peak current density of approximately -1.70 mA/cm 2 . Longer deposition times showed decreased performance.

title: Novel Strategy for Functional Oligopeptide Conjugation inside the Mesopores of Silica Nanoparticles
abstract: The functionalization of mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNPs) with biomolecule-selective oligopeptides is an important method for materials design in bio-separations, drug delivery, and other biotechnology applications. MSNPs are desirable for these applications because their flexible and well-controlled synthesis process provides well-defined pore spaces with high surface areas and pore volumes. MSNPs provide a unique protective microenvironment for binding between target biomolecules and conjugated polypeptides. However, procedures specifically designed for oligopeptide attachment within the pores of MSNPs still need to be developed to avoid uncontrolled reactions at the external particle surface. Here, a functionalization process is described involving a diazirine-based hetero-bifunctional linker, sulfo-succinimidyl 6-(4,4’ azipentanamido) hexanoate (sulfo-NHS-LC-diazirine). This linker allows for controlled attachment of oligopeptides to the surface of the MSNPs (average pore diameter of 8 nm and surface area of 730 m 2 /g) that have been functionalized with amine (-NH 2 ) groups by condensation of aminopropyltriethoxysilane. The choice of hetero-bifunctional linker allows for specific control over whether sulfo-NHS reacts first with the peptide N-terminus or the amine groups on the surface. It is found that peptide-first attachment (reacting sulfo-NHS first with the peptide N-terminus) leads to more efficient conjugation because this approach allows for diffusion of the linker-peptide conjugate to the interior of the particle pores before attachment by UV activation of the diazirine group. This is quantified using the fluorescein isothiocyanate-tagged tetrapeptide arginine-serine-serine-valine (RSSV) to give 0.5 mol peptide/mol amine. To demonstrate the versatility of the approach, three distinct oligopeptides (RSSV, Glycine-Glycine-Glycine-Glycine (4G), and a 16-mer composed of four repeated RSSV units) are conjugated by peptide-first attachment to the surface of the MSNPs. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) shows similar degrees of conjugation for all three peptides, suggesting versatility and generalizability of the procedure developed. Finally, these peptide-conjugated nanoparticles are used as a high-capacity adsorbent for β-estradiol (representative of the broad estrogen family) to show specific binding activity above that of MSNPs without conjugated peptides. This study has implications for utilizing oligopeptide-functionalized MSNPs for bioactive molecule separation from living cells (nanoharvesting) or adsorption for environmental remediation (removal of endocrine disruptors from wastewater).

title: Production of Monodisperse Yolk-Shell Titanium Dioxide Microspheres with Tunable Characteristics
abstract: Titanium dioxide is a photocatalytic material that has proven useful in the degradation of organic pollutants. In turn, this photocatalyst may prove useful in efforts to handle common greenhouse gases more sustainably. One possible application for the use of TiO 2 in photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants could possibly be a bi-reforming reaction of carbon dioxide and methane into synthesis gas. By degrading these greenhouse gases into synthesis gas, the product gas mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen can be used in the synthesis of hydrocarbon fuels through Fischer-Tropsch reactions. Through this reaction, greenhouse gases may be recycled into useful liquid fuels. Without the use of a photocatalyst, the high reaction enthalpy associated with the aforementioned reforming reaction (247 kJ/mol) renders the reaction non-feasible. However, the implementation of TiO 2 as a photocatalyst may aid significantly in lowering heat energy requirement of the reaction. Unfortunately, the commercially available TiO 2 photocatalyst, Degussa P25, is a mixed phase polydisperse nanopowder with an anatase/rutile phase ratio of 85:15. The high degree of polydispersity coupled with the very small average size of these nanoparticles would result in undesirably dense packing and a high pressure drop across a packed bed reforming reactor which creates obstacles to achieving desirable throughputs at atmospheric pressure. In order to solve this issue, TiO z microparticles with a high degree of monodispersity needed to be manufactured while maintaining or exceeding the specific surface areas of Degussa P25. This work explores the design and production of highly monodisperse TiO 2 microparticles with tunable size, surface morphology, surface areas, and phase ratios. The particles were manufactured in a flow-focusing microreactor composed of three different capillaries that takes advantage of the immiscibility of two feed solutions to create monodisperse droplets prior to the hydrolysis reaction. The continuous phase is a hydrophilic solution containing 1 wt% Pluronic F108 (a surfactant) in formamide, while the dispersed phase is a hydrophobic solution composed of toluene, a photocurable polymer, titanium n-butoxide, and a photoinitiator. The droplets formed by two-phase flow through the outlet capillary are collected in water containing surfactant and subsequently photocured, washed, dried, and calcined. This work has shown that the aforementioned characteristics can be adjusted by varying hydrolysis conditions, precursor composition, and calcination temperatures. In this way, it has been possible to design microparticles suitable for use in photocatalysis of greenhouse gas reforming reactions.

title: Additive Manufacturing with Semi-Crystalline Thermoplastics: Properties for Printability
abstract: Temperature control is an integral part of success in 3D printing. Slight changes in printing conditions can drastically affect the printed part. This project is aimed to investigate the thermal properties of common semi-crystalline 3D printing thermoplastics in fused filament fabrication (FFF) with thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) and polylactic acid (PLA). Melt flow behavior of the filaments was studied by printing lines on the printer bed to determine the mass flow rate over a range of nozzle temperatures from a high temperature of 255⁰C to the values where no filament is extruded by 2⁰C increments. The time remained constant throughout the experiments for each filament. However, the mass flow rate drastically decreased as the nozzle temperature dropped below 209⁰C and 183⁰C for TPU and PLA, respectively. Filament behavior changed with nozzle temperature, so while the filaments could be extruded at lower than manufacturer suggested temperatures, the overall printability is drastically reduced below a certain threshold of nozzle temperature. This behavior is attributed to change in melting range of the polymers with the heating rate. Therefore, the data was compared to DSC measurements at different heating rates to better understand the range of melting temperatures of the semi-crystalline polymers. This data can be used to achieve more successful 3D prints and an overall better understanding of printing behaviors at various temperatures.

title: Development of Accurate Eam Potentials of Gold with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: One of the most critical limitations to performing successful molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of metal structures in many fields of study is the availability of suitable interatomic potentials. Embedded atom potentials (EAM) in particular provide a unique solution due to their low computational cost and ability to accurately model bulk properties of pure metals and their alloys. Many EAM potential parameters for gold have been developed to reproduce experimental and/or quantum calculations data. However, when these parameters are used to simulate systems beyond their calibrated environments, the data presented can be invalid or open to interpretation. We present accurate EAM interatomic potentials for gold that was developed to reproduce its experimental properties by integrating particle swarm optimization (PSO) with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The resulting EAM parameters of gold were validated by performing Bayesian uncertainty quantification. Overall, these new parameters of gold are robust and transferable across a range of different conditions. The interactions between these new gold parameters and water were also developed to reproduce its interfacial tension at 300 K.

title: An Improved Characterization of Topological Features in Molecular Simulations Using Persistent Homology.
abstract: We apply a mathematical method known as persistent homology to analyze the geometrical features of mesophases produced from molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, we study ionic liquid/hydrocarbon mixtures. Ionic liquids (ILs) are salts with unique properties, which have made them ideally suited for many applications. Their ability to dissolve different, sometimes amphiphilic, compounds is likely tied to the formation of segregated nanoscale domains. These domains, or aggregates, are created due to the separation of the polar and nonpolar regions in the ionic liquid. Determining the shape of these domains is very important in understanding the behavior of the system. Persistent homology uses a process known as filtration that incorporates a geometric measurement into topological invariants. By using a filtration parameter, simplicial complexes, such as triangles, are generated. The lifespans of the invariants are then recorded in a barcode. Such barcodes can be interpreted to determine the geometry of the object. Persistent homology was tested on objects with well-defined shapes, providing an understanding of the detailed barcode resulting from the analysis, such as the interpretation of the lifetime of lines in the barcode and the different dimensions. Comparisons between the shapes of these mesophases was done via persistent homology using the bottleneck distance to determine how similar two topologies are from one another. The smaller the value of the bottleneck distance, the more similarity exists between the two shapes. Additionally, persistent homology can be used to analyze different properties, such as thickness and diameter, of 2D and 3D shapes to see how each property affects the barcode. Such tests gave an insight on how persistent homology works, allowing us to use it on systems of ionic liquids to quantitatively characterize their topology. Multiple simulations containing the mixtures of lipid-inspired ILs with either hexane or cyclohexane were conducted at various mole fractions and analyzed. The barcodes from each simulation showed that increasing the concentration of IL in the system increases the number of aggregates in both 2D and 3D. Furthermore, most holes generally appear to have the same size, suggesting a characteristic size that the IL aggregates like to adopt. Future studies will compare these simulated IL aggregates with a library of idealized shapes to identify its characteristic shape. Moreover, work will be done to extend the persistent homology code to accurately deal with topologies extending across periodic boundaries.

title: Packing Density and Thermoresponsive Morphology of PNIPAM-Co-PAA Microgel Coatings
abstract: Microgels that alter their size or shape in response to external stimuli such as temperature, pH, and light are gaining considerable attention for their application potential in “smart” membrane technologies. By analyzing microgel depositions on solid substrates, one could better understand how these microgels deposit and function which is critical to advancing their implementation. This study investigates the effects that temperature and pH have on the deposition density of poly[(N-isopropylacrylamide)-co-(acrylic acid)] hydrogels and seeks to find a relationship between density and functional surface roughness change. The microgels were deposited upon silicon wafers primed with poly(octadecene-alt-maleic anhydride) and polyethyleneimine which created monolayer systems. The POMA layer provided a strong base layer due the 18-carbon tail hydrophobic interaction with the wafer. The branched PEI then reacted with POMA’s anhydrides which provided a top layer that was abundant with hydrogen bonding sites for the microgels. Microgels were deposited via spin-coating and incubation at temperatures both below and above the lower critical solution temperature of pNIPAm. Optical imaging and Matlab software were used to determine the densities of the monolayer systems, while a laser scanning microscope and MultiFile Analyzer software determined the microgel surface roughness upon temperature change. As could be expected, temperature and pH played a key role in how the microgel adherence to the solid substrate: increasing temperature and pH showed a positive correlation with density measurements. Following, a relationship was also observed between the density and the temperature associated surface roughness change. Overall, deposition conditions and methods have profound effects on surface morphology that can be qualitatively and quantitively described and related to functional surface roughness change.

title: Development of a Rechargeable Antimicrobial Textile
abstract: Functionalizing cotton with antimicrobial properties shows promise for applications in hospitals, for the military, and the general public. There has been a great deal of attention paid to methods of attaching n-halamine compounds to textiles for this purpose. Over time, the halogens present on these compounds dissociate into the surrounding environment and function as biocides. After dissociation, the n-halamines can be recharged by exposure to a solution containing halogen ions. One such n-halamine is 5,5-dimethylhydantoin (DMH), which is commonly brominated to a biocidal form for water purification. Previously in this project, a procedure for the synthesizing and purifying a DMH derivative, allyl-5,5-dimethylhadantion (ADMH), had been optimized. This compound retains the antimicrobial functionality of DMH, yet also can be chemically bonded to cotton. Once bonded, the strength of the antimicrobial properties was evaluated by exposing the fabric to the bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Serratia marcescens and observing the growth inhibition in comparison to a positive and a negative control. Currently, tests have shown bacterial growth inhibition on only the fabric surface, suggesting that no chlorine is leaching into the environment surrounding the sample. This is desirable since skin irritation is noted as a possible drawback of using chlorinated n-halamines. Previous work on this project followed a “bottom-up” approach to the fabric modification; each necessary molecule is added to the fabric individually concluding with ADMH and its chlorination. This process does not allow for quantitative assessment each reaction’s efficiency. It is desired to produce the final biocide in solution so that it may be attached in a single step which is ideal for synthesis on an industrial scale. Thus far, the molecule that links ADMH to the fabric has been synthesized and precipitated out via acidification. No IR spectroscopy data exists for the linker currently, and therefore this route of analysis has been performed by matching peaks with bonds known to exist on the linker. The final goal of this project is to develop a water-soluble molecule for which the process of synthesis and fabric attachment can be easily scaled up. This allows the treated fabric to be available to a wide range of consumers and may be implemented in a variety of fields where textiles are in continual contact with skin.

title: Developing Evanescent Wave Scattering As a Tool for Tracking Janus Particle Dynamics in Response to Electric Fields
abstract: Colloidal particles are a highly diverse class of materials that can be observed in numerous applications ranging from ventilation systems to food processing. Colloidal particles can also be fabricated to function as models for more complex systems of biological or mechanical interest to study and characterize their behavior in controlled experimental conditions. Our research focuses on developing evanescent wave scattering as a sensitive technique for measuring small fluctuations in the dynamics of “patchy” and “Janus” colloids with 30% and 50% coverage, respectively. These particles were observed at equilibrium and under the influence of an applied AC electric field. Scattering intensity was analyzed prior to and after application of the electric field to determine what influence this external field had on position and orientation dynamics. Probability distributions were prepared to test the hypothesis that translational and rotational dynamics are influenced by application of an electric field. Due to the characteristic surface coverage of these colloids causing distinct scattering patterns, bimodal distributions in the data were used to suggest unique orientational dynamics. Our results also suggest that a Janus particle will move to a smaller most probable height upon application of an AC electric field.

title: Incorporation of Allograft into Chitosan Hydrogels for Treatment of Vertebral Compression Fractures
abstract: In the United States, 1.5 million osteoporotic fractures occur annually, almost half of which are vertebral compression fractures (VCFs). Currently, the most common non-invasive treatment options for addressing VCFs are kyphoplasty and vertebroplasty. These both include the injection of poly(methyl)methacrylate (PMMA), which is non-biodegradable and has much higher compressive strength than native bone, resulting in an increased risk of adjacent future fractures. We have been exploring chitosan hydrogels as a potential replacement for these established treatments. Chitosan hydrogels have become widely used for tissue engineering applications due to their injectability, biodegradability, and bioactivity; however, poor mechanical properties are an apparent disadvantage of these biomaterials. Recently, a combination of physical and chemical crosslinking (with carbonate and genipin, respectively) as well as physical incorporation of cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) have been shown to produce hydrogels with desirable degradability and low toxicity. Furthermore, incorporation of calcium phosphates into these biomaterials facilitates the release of calcium ions (Ca 2+ ) and phosphate ions (P i ) within their osteoinductive therapeutic window, conveying desirable bone-developing bioactivity. Calcium phosphate incorporation was also found to increase hydrogel compressive strength. Though promising, these hydrogels are still significantly weaker than native bone tissue, leaving them unsuitable for load bearing applications. Recently, we have incorporated crushed cancellous allograft (MTF Biologics) to address this issue. Our results show that these novel complex hydrogels possess physical properties similar to those of healthy bone tissue. In vitro studies will be performed on murine mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to test the biocompatibility and osteoinductivity of the allograft/hydrogel composite. Additionally, mass loss, swelling, and compressive strength studies will be conducted to ensure that the hydrogels have desirable ion release profiles and mechanical properties for VCF repair applications. It is expected that these complex hydrogels will have the same osteoinductive properties as the original hydrogels while also having the improved strength necessary to support load bearing bone regeneration.

title: Continuous Viral Purification Using an Aqueous Two-Phase System
abstract: Current methods and ordering of bioproduct separation processes are driven by purity, yield, and activity requirements. After inoculation, bioseparation processes are long, sequential unit operations including filtration, extraction, and chromatography. The downstream process of viral products currently accounts for 70% of production overhead with a 30% acceptance yield. Our goal is to improve viral purification techniques with a continuous Aqueous Two-Phase System (ATPS) that produces a higher yield, lower cost, and faster production. ATPS is a liquid-liquid partitioning formed by mixing two immiscible aqueous solutions. Our methods involves the continuous processes of a parvovirus with ATPS, followed by membrane separation. Based on previous experiments, the critical concentration of ATPS components, polyethylene glycol (PEG) and citrate, were pumped continuously and spiked with porcine parvovirus (PPV). Virus hydrophobicity and electrostatic interaction are used as driving forces to concentrate viral particle impurities into the bottom phase and virus into the top phase of the ATPS system. To capture and isolate the product, extraction of PEG from 9 log PPV by ultrafiltration (UF) is being explored as a potential final polishing step. Varied psi and PEG concentrations were tested to find optimal recovery to be applied in the design of the continuous process. PPV virulence and structural integrity determined by qualitative (TEM or DLS) and quantitative (MTT assay) measure. The results from our experiments can be used to show that ATPS is successful at purifying viruses continuously with potential to incorporate into the manufacturing of viral therapeutic products.

title: A Bead-Based Microfluidic Testbed for an Enhanced Lab-on-a-Chip Device for Shear Enhanced Purification of Biomolecules
abstract: Protein purification is cumbersome, expensive and requires a number of steps. Post purification, the process equipment often requires extensive, costly maintenance that needs harsh chemicals. Here, we present a new methodology of using shear forces that offers an alternative approach to protein purification that reduces the number of steps, making it easier, greener, scalable and cheaper. Analogous to affinity chromatography, a stationary phase – Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs) - will be used to purify proteins. Protein A will be attached to CNTs using EDC-NHS chemistry. Post attachment, CNT’s will be tightly packed in a microfluidic channel (akin to a packed bed reactor) and are immobilized (against the fluidic drag force) by a transverse electric field from non-planar interdigitated electrodes. At low flow rates, the target proteins (monoclonal antibodies) attach to Protein A while the rest of the solution flows by (filtration). The flow rate is then suitably modified to increase the shear force enough to release the biomolecules from the CNT complex into an elution buffer while maintaining their bio-functionality (purification). Hence, the shear force approach drastically reduces the number of steps required for the desired purification. Post elution buffer, prolonged washing with a solution allows us to regenerate the CNT’s for the next round of purification. To develop optimal conjugation protocols for the process, the whole attachment of protein A to separation has to be done in situ. We have created a testbed with 1 µm carboxylated silica particles to mimic the CNT. Unlike CNT (quencher), silica particles allow us optical (fluorescence) visualization. We have studied in detail the effect of fluid flow, pH, and temperature on the purification efficacy of our platform using fluorescent antibodies. Further the in-situ protocols for EDC-NHS functionalization, antibody attachment and stripping has also been studied using different fluorescent antibodies. The optimization on the silica beads allowed us to translate to a CNT based device which offers tremendous enhancement in shear force among others. We believe that this technology not only benefits the protein manufacturing scene in general (i.e., production of mainstream proteins such as insulin), but also other contemporary, specific applications such as using monoclonal antibodies from cancer treatment to sensors.

title: Liquid-Liquid Equilibria Studies of Potential Organic Solvents As Ethanol Extractants from Aqueous Solutions
abstract: Recent years have brought concern for the environment to the forefront, specifically with negative impacts of fossil fuels. Jet fuels are estimated to contribute to 2% of CO 2 emissions and are predicted to rise. Many alternatives to petroleum based fuels are being explored, including biofuels which have the potential to reduce CO 2 emissions by 85%. However, biofuels do not come without challenges. Inevitably, these fuels will have high water content, due to water formed during biological reactions. Unfortunately, water can be damaging to engines, requiring removal for optimum performance rates. Hydrocarbons, such as ethanol, have unideal interactions with water, forming an azeotrope, and cannot be fully separated via simple chemical engineering separations such as distillation, making the process highly energy-intensive and expensive. Liquid-liquid extraction could be a more cost-effective solution, with a proper solvent, because it can be implemented with smaller equipment and lower energy consumption. This project analyzes the effectiveness of using three green, organic solvents: castor oil, dodecane, and 2-methylcyclohexanol, to extract ethanol from water. Liquid-liquid equilibrium was determined using the cloud point method and data for the three ternary systems was collected using headspace gas chromatography at 25°C. A ternary diagram for each organic solvent, water, and ethanol was obtained. Preliminary liquid-liquid extractions using a laboratory scale mixer-settler were used to compare the effectiveness of each solvent in separation ethanol from the aqueous stream. Parameters gleaned from the ternary systems and the preliminary liquid-liquid extractions studies were used to analyze the potency of each solvent in the separation of ethanol. Ultimately, this work provides new insights into the use of green solvents as possible ethanol extraction agents in liquid-liquid extractions processes.

title: Non-Enveloped Virus Purification Using Cation Exchange Chromatography
abstract: The supply of vaccines is not consistent and can leave countries without access to lifesaving vaccines. Companies are leaving the market due to multifactorial production issues which leaves countries without access to vaccinations. Vaccine manufacturer’s ability to make pure and potent vaccines depend directly on the capability to purify viruses without a decrease in yield. Currently, chromatography is the most common method in industry to purify bioproducts because of its versatility. The mode that is most used for viral purification is ion exchange chromatography. Currently, anion exchange chromatography (AEX) is used more often in virus purification. AEX allows negatively charged viruses to bind to a positively charged chromatography surface at neutral pH, where viruses are the most stable. However, cation exchange chromatography (CEX) has the potential for improved purity. All forms of chromatography share the same basic steps: equilibration, loading, elution, washing, and regeneration. CEX uses two forms of elution, increasing salt gradients or increasing pH gradients. The more common of the two is the salt gradient because of its simplicity and reliability. However, virus elution yields are often low with salt gradients due to the variability of the viral surface. Gradients using a change in pH exploit the biomolecule’s isoelectric point (pI). pH gradients are more complex to design but have the potential to provide the necessary separation to rapidly purify vaccine products. The non-enveloped virus porcine parvovirus (PPV), with a reported pI of 5, was purified with CEX. PPV was loaded at pH 3.5 and eluted with a pH step gradient. High recovery of virus particles was found during the elution step of pH 6 with high concentration of the virus eluting over the duration of the pH 6 step. Purity analysis demonstrated a removal of 92% contaminating protein and 98% DNA. Future work will comprise of purification of different viruses and increasing loading volumes to concentrate products. This research will result in improved methods of purification that will bring new vaccines and gene therapy vectors to market and keep costs low.

title: Green Solvent Extraction of Soy Biomass
abstract: Biofeedstocks contain a variety of components that can be used as fuels or as value-added chemicals and are of particular interest in the energy, pharmaceutical, and nutraceutical industries. Solvent extraction is a useful and well-developed means of extracting many of these components. Because solvents account for a considerable portion of process waste, it is important that green solvents (solvents with fewer environmental, health, and safety impacts), are used to extract these products . In this work, a variety of green solvents were used to extract triglycerides and phospholipids from two biofeedstocks, soy lecithin and soybean flour . The components in each extract were analyzed using supercritical fluid chromatography-mass spectrometry in order to determine the extraction efficiency and selectivity of each solvent. Overall, it is seen that certain solvents, such as acetone and ethyl acetate, were more selective towards triglycerides than phospholipids while other solvents, such as 2-methylhudrofuran, were more selective towards phospholipids than triglycerides. These results make it easier to select a particular solvent when carrying out a solvent extraction based on the yields of the component needed in an extract. In addition, this work analyzes the properties of each solvent to allow for predicti on of the effectiveness of other solvent s with similar properties in order to aid in the selection of solvents for extraction processes.

title: Comparing the Efficacy of Enveloped Virus and Non-Enveloped Virus Purification in Aqueous Two-Phase System
abstract: The existing need of viral vaccines in the less developed regions and growing demand for gene therapy vectors and oncolytic virus therapy has demanded the biopharma companies to upgrade the current production strategies. Downstream processing to purify viral particles from the host cell contaminants is one of the major contributors to not only limiting the throughput but also cost of vaccine production. Current methods based on chromatography and filtration are facing a major challenge to meet the required high yield production. Aqueous two-phase system (ATPS) has been identified as one of the potential candidates to address these issues in the vaccine manufacturing. ATPS formed by two partially miscible aqueous solutions can be composed of polymer-polymer or polymer-salt. However, the discrepancy in understanding the biomolecule partitioning mechanism has stalled the industrial implementation. Our previous study with porcine parvovirus, a non-enveloped virus, has inferred that two major forces, hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions, drive viral particles and contaminant proteins to the opposite phases in a polyethylene glycol (PEG, MW 12000 Da) and citrate salt system. This work explores the purification of structurally different category of viruses than the previous study to generalize the notion of above-mentioned driving forces and reduce the experimental space to optimize the purification. This study used model enveloped virus (herpes simplex virus, HSV-1), which has an extra bilipid membrane around the protein capsid enclosing the genetic material. The recovery of the virus in the PEG-rich phase was studied with an increasing PEG and citrate concentrations at various tie line lengths to study the partitioning behavior of viruses. Further, water structure amending compounds, osmolytes (glycine, betaine, and TMAO), were included in the system to compare the enhanced driving forces to boost the purification at lower compositions. The results from our experiment can be used to provide higher virus recovery and help lower overall vaccine production cost .

title: Aminopropylsiloxane Networks for Regenerative Carbon Capture Sorbents
abstract: With over half of the world’s energy generated from the combustion of fossil fuels, the demand for developments in carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) capture technology has surged over the last decade. The end goal for captured CO 2 is to utilize it by chemically converting it into value-added products. Currently, amine sorbents are the most prominent and effective mechanism for sequestering CO 2 at both high and low concentrations. Historically, liquid amines have been used for adsorption of CO 2 from flue gas on the commercial scale. However, aqueous sorbents capture CO 2 by the physical formation of bonds (physisorption), therefore requiring more energy to regenerate the sorbent compared to a solid sorbent that adsorbs CO 2 by chemisorption. Currently, research efforts are focused on increasing the adsorption capacity of solid materials in order to be cost-efficient and comparable to that of aqueous capacities. Here, a silica-supported, solid sorbent was functionalized with propan-1-amine groups using aminopropylsiloxane networks. Nitrogen loading on the sorbent was measured using a LECO elemental analyzer. Absolute CO 2 adsorption capacity was obtained by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). Monolayer uptake measurements, corresponding to active surface area of the sample, were taken by a Quantachrome Gas Sorption Analyzer. Monolayer uptake and nitrogen content were compared to gain an understanding of the aminopropylsiloxane assembly and active site availability to incoming gas. Thermal cycling stability of the sorbents was also characterized using TGA to test the sorbent’s ability to regenerate active surface area upon CO 2 desorption. These solid sorbents are considered “low temperature” with adsorption and desorption steps both occurring at temperatures lower than 200°C. Sorbents with different mass loadings of nitrogen and varying functional group length were analyzed and compared.

title: Effect of Incomplete Purging on Carbon Capture By Pressure Swing Adsorption with High-Pressure Rinsing
abstract: Pressure swing adsorption (PSA) has the potential to be used for post-combustion CO 2 capture, as well as CO 2 capture from other gas sources. However, carbon capture based on adsorbent equilibrium selectivity is not viable with basic PSA cycle scheduling since recovery of reasonably pure CO 2 requires pressure ratios which are unrealistically large and expensive. High-pressure rinsing is required to remove residual air from the bed prior to blowdown, ensuring the recovery of pure CO 2 at more moderate pressure ratios. The process with rinsing might still be improved by leveraging an incomplete purge, using a volume of sweep gas less than the minimum needed to ensure a clean bed, which has been known to improve recovery in O 2 and N 2 production. title: Engineering Membrane Adsorbers for Pfas Mitigation from Water
abstract: Per - and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and related compounds such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) are labeled as persistent organic pollutants by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). PFAS were used in firefighting foam, non - stick cookware, waterproof outdoor gear, food packaging , and more. PFAS have contaminated the drinking water supply of many countries around the world, including the US . Acc ording to the EPA , PFAS accumulate and stay in the human body for l ong periods of time and are harmful to the body’s reproductive and immunological systems . In 2019 , the EPA recommends PFAS levels of no more than 70 ppt in drinking water and million s of people in the US are regularly drinking water contaminated with more than this level . There is a need to effectively and efficiently remove PFAS compounds from drinking water. Currently g ranular activated carbon and i on - exchang e/non - ion - exchange polymers in the form of resin beads are used to adsorb PFAS from water in water treatment plants . T he se methods u tilize diffusive flow to adsorb PFAS which is a slow process . Nanofiltration and reverse osmosis can also be used to remove PFAS from water but are expensive to perform due to pressure requirements . If membrane adsorbers utiliz ing convective flow were able to effectively capture PFAS from water they would enable a new treatment technique for PFAS mitigation. This would allow th e adsorption of PFAS to be regulated by slightly pressurizing the contaminated water to pas s it through the membrane, resulting in a more efficient method of purification . Polyethersulfone membranes w ere utilized to remove sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) , a surrogate of PFAS, from water . UV photopolymerization w as utilized to graft a polymer layer from the membrane surface . 2 - [( m ethacryloyloxy)ethyl]trimethylammonium chloride (MOETMA), 2 - ( d imethylamino)ethyl methacrylate (DMAEMA) , 4 - v inylpyridine, and b utyl a crylate (spacer molecule) were the polymers experimented with. The membranes were tested with and without the addition of a cross - linker , m ethylenebis(acrylamide) (MBAA) , which acts to stabilize the adsorbing polymer chains on the surface of the membrane. B romoethane was used to quaternize poly( 4 - v inylpyridine ) . The positively charged polymer chains allow ed the membrane to adsorb the negatively charged SDS from solution. Each membrane was flux tested to determine if modification was successful. ATR - FTIR spectroscopy w as used to determine the extent of modification. C ontact angle goniometry w as used to determine the effect of modification on the hydrophilicity of the membrane. Static adsorption testing was done to determine the membrane adsorption capacity for SDS.

title: Graphene Oxide Membranes: Synthesis Methods, Unique Properties, and Potential for Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) Removal
abstract: Graphene oxide (GO) creates a thin membrane with tight interlayer spacing that allows it to maintain high permeability along with high particle selectivity. A GO membrane was created using a vacuum filtration cell to cast a dilute, aqueous solution of graphene oxide onto a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF200) substrate. A GO membrane with a 33% decrease in graphene oxide loading showed decreased membrane thickness, increased permeability, and decreased rejection of dextrose molecules suggesting that the incidence of defects increased when GO loading was reduced. The graphene oxide adopted a negative charge at any pH above ~3.5 and exhibited a maximum negative zeta potential of -22.5 mV at pH=8.2. Graphene oxide’s negative surface charge in neutral water, improves its rejection of negatively charged particles such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) by charge repulsion. PFOA is a harmful, biologically persistent compound that contaminates water supplies, particularly near chemical plants where it is manufactured or disposed of. PFOA rejection was found to be highest in a high pH solution with a low PFOA concentration. The GO membrane rejected 58% of a 20-ppm PFOA solution in distilled water (pH=7) but rejection increased to 75% when a 1-ppm PFOA solution was used in the same conditions. It is predicted that lower concentrations of PFOA, like those present in drinking water, could achieve near complete rejection. When a lower pH solution (pH 3) was used, the retention appeared to be nearly as high, but the “rejection” proved to be entirely due to adsorption on the membrane surface based on a large disparity in the mass balance. PFOA rejection dropped to 15% when tested in a 90/10 isopropanol solvent with 1 ppm PFOA concentration, suggesting that charge plays a major role in rejection.

title: The Effect of Calcination Extent on Sorbent Utilization in Calcium Looping
abstract: Calcium looping is a promising carbon capture technology, circulating CaO-based sorbents between carbonator and calciner units. Natural limestone is a popular choice for the sorbent material due to its abundance and low cost. However, rapid sorbent deactivation is a major challenge to the long-term stable operation of the calcium looping system. Previous studies have mostly focused on the decay of utilization of fully calcined sorbents over multiple cycles of carbonation/calcination. However, lime-based sorbents are rarely fully calcined in practical operations and, hence, the effect of partial calcination on sorbent cyclic performance is of interest. This work investigates the effect of the extent of limestone calcination on sorbent utilization decay over multiple cycles. Greymont limestone particles (510-700 µm in diameter) were calcined and carbonated for 20 successive cycles in a thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA). The extent of calcination was varied by changing the calcination time, with the calcination time being fixed for each cyclic test. It was observed that partial calcination results in enhanced sorbent utilization over the testing cycles. The experimental results give better understanding of the mechanism of sorbent utilization decay, while also providing more experimental support for prospective calcination kinetics modelling. Future study will verify the observed effects of partial calcination for prolonged numbers of cycles and different calcination operating conditions.

title: Self-Regulating Forward Osmosis-Reverse Osmosis Hybrid System
abstract: Self-Regulating Forward Osmosis-Reverse Osmosis Hybrid System Colin Fitzsimonds, Noah Ferguson, Dr. Jeffrey McCutcheon Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT Although reverse osmosis (RO) is a commonly used desalination technology, the susceptibility of these membranes to foul makes them challenging to operate in wastewater reuse applications. Pretreatment of these feed solutions is one method of reducing the fouling of RO membranes. Such systems often significantly increase the footprint of the desalination plant and the CAPEX for construction. Using forward osmosis (FO) as a pretreatment method in a hybridized system has been considered as an alternative method to dealing with difficult to treat feed waters. The potential complexities to balancing the fluxes between the FO and RO systems and overall uncertainty about the operation of these systems act as a deterrent to their use in a desalination plant. In this work, we demonstrate self-regulating behavior that could allay fears of needing complex process control regimes in these types of hybridized systems. We demonstrate this behavior using a module-scale testing system that mirrors the behavior of a larger scale system. The system shows flux convergence between the FO and RO modules when disrupted by a sudden change in the RO module pressure and therefore does not require complex controls to ensure flux convergence between the two processes.

title: Low-Cost Microfluidic Devices for Bio-Separation Applications
abstract: Single-use vessels have gained significant popularity in the biological processing industry. In this work, we develop software and process equipment for manufacturing a single use or recyclable separation device for the extraction of DNA from solution. Additional software is developed to control the extraction process. Separation units consist of submillimeter expansion-contraction channels, fabricated from machined thermoplastics using a low-cost (<$200) micro-mill. The mill is controlled by a Raspberry Pi, running a homebrew Python code which generates and streams commands to the mill. The separation of DNA from solution is achieved by Electrohydrodynamic Migration, in which DNA molecules are stretched into cigar-shaped conformations by the shearing forces generated by the Poiseuille flow, with the long axis tilted towards the center of the confining channel. An electric field, applied counter to the flow, then has the effect of selectively driving the DNA towards the channel walls. Near the walls, the motion of the DNA is dominated by electrophoresis, which returns the molecules to the inlet of the device. The process leads to a selective concentration of DNA in a small region around the beginning of the contraction. Separation and concentration require precise control of the applied voltage and pressure differences which are achieved by Arduino microcontrollers controlled via serial connections by a Python interface. Using Python for experimental control allows for reproducible experiments, by saving the controlling instructions as ladder logic in text files. Additionally, the Python interface allows for real-time analysis of the images gathered by the microscope camera, which can be used to fine tune the experiment via application of feedback controls.

title: Temperature Swing Adsorption of Perfluoroorganics By Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) Hydrogels and Membranes
abstract: This research is aimed at evaluating the effect of temperature on the removal of perfluoroorganic compounds in water filtration. Polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) microfiltration membranes are functionalized with poly-N-isopropylacrylamide (PNIPAAm), and its temperature responsive behavior is studied as it relates to water flux and adsorption/desorption of perfluorochemicals. PNIPAAm has a relatively low Lower Critical Solution Temperature (LCST) of around 32°C, which makes it appealing for industrial use. PNIPAAm has a sharp transition from hydrophilic behavior below its LCST to hydrophobic behavior above its LCST, thus, when the PNIPAAm is exhibiting hydrophobic behavior, it retracts/collapses upon itself in an aqueous environment. In doing so, the isopropyl groups dehydrate first, causing the polymer chain to collapse, thus causing hydrophobic contaminants to partition into that domain. Reversely, bringing the temperature down past the LCST will rehydrate the isopropyl groups, which reduces adsorption and allows desorption to occur. The stability and reusability of these membranes are demonstrated as well. Specifically, this study’s goal is to evaluate the feasibility of temperature swing adsorption/desorption of Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in water filtration. This research is supported by the NIEHSSRP grant P42ES007380, and by the NSF KY EPSCOR program. Full-scale PVDF membranes were developed through collaborative work with Nanostone-Sepro (Oceanside, CA, USA).

title: Direct CO2 Capture from Air Using Poly(ethylenimine)-Loaded Polymer/Silica Fiber Sorbents
abstract: Direct CO 2 capture from atmospheric air is gaining increased attention as one of the most scalable negative carbon approaches available to tackle climate change if coupled with the sequestration of CO 2 geologically. Furthermore, it can also provide CO 2 for further utilization from a globally uniform source, which is especially advantageous for economies without natural sources of carbon-based feedstocks. Solid-supported amine-based materials are e ff ective for direct air capture (DAC) due to their high CO 2 uptakes and acceptable sorption kinetics at ambient temperature. In this work, we describe the application of polymer/silica fi ber sorbents functionalized with a primary amine-rich polymer, poly(ethylenimine) (PEI), for DAC. Monolithic fi ber sorbents composed of cellulose acetate and SiO 2 are synthesized via the dry-jet, wet quench spinning technique. These fi bers are then functionalized with PEI (M w 800 Da) in a simple and scalable postspinning infusion step and tested for CO 2 capture under pseudoequilibrium conditions as well as under breakthrough conditions. An investigation to study the e ff ect of feed fl ow rate, adsorption temperature, and presence of moisture in the feed on the CO 2 breakthrough performance of a densely packed fi ber sorbent module is conducted to highlight the potential application of this class of structured contactors in direct air capture. The pressure drop of these contactors at high gas velocities is also evaluated. Finally, a vacuum-assisted desorption step is demonstrated for production of high-purity CO 2 from both dry and humid ambient air mixtures.

title: Fabrication of a Novel Reactive Membrane for Degradation of Polyfluorinated Compounds
abstract: Nanomaterials are typically used in the field of membrane technology to impart a desired characteristic on the membrane so as to enhance selectivity of the membrane and increase the life span of the membrane. Photocatalytic membrane processes generate oxygen-reactive radicals under irradiation by light that could degrade pollutants in feed solutions. Phosphorene is a recently discovered two-dimensional material that shows great promise as a photocatalyst because it can generate reactive oxygen species (singlet oxygen, hydroxyl radicals and superoxide radicals). The main objective of this collaborative research is to develop and validate environmentally safe nanomaterial-based approaches for treatment of drinking water including degradation of per- and polyfluorinated chemicals (PFAS). PFAS are surfactant chemicals commonly found in household and commercial products, but they are also very persistent in the environment and are known human carcinogens. They are very resistant to traditional drinking water treatment technologies and hence a reactive membrane that can degrade and remove these harmful chemicals during the treatment process will be worthwhile. Specifically, we aim to study the in vivo toxicity of phosphorene in its free form and in filtrates after nanoparticles are embedded into the membrane on C. elegans mortality, reproduction, behavior and antioxidant responses. Among PFAS that will be used, are representatives of long-chain PFAS including perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA), and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) as well as newer short-chain PFASs, such as GenX. In this research, phosphorene will be fabricated by the liquid exfoliation of black phosphorus. Membranes will be made via the non-solvent induced phase separation technique. Phosphorene will be physically incorporated into the membrane. The membranes will be characterized using several microscopic and analytical techniques and finally tested for the degradation of PFAS in solution.

title: The Modeling and Measurement of Solute Solubility and Partitioning for a Hybrid Supercritical Fluid/Ionic Liquid Extraction Process
abstract: Chemical separation is an important aspect of chemical engineering, and many techniques for these processes are large energy sinks and produce a lot of waste. Ionic liquid enhanced supercritical fluid extraction is one way to reduce both the energy required and waste produced. Ionic liquids (ILs) are organic salts that have a melting point of 100°C or below and have practically no vapor pressure. Supercritical fluids (SCF) are compounds that are above both their critical temperature and pressure. These compounds have gas-like transport properties and liquid-like solvation properties. Both ILs and SCFs can be tuned to perform specific tasks. IL’s ions can be modified by changing the functional groups to alter certain properties like solvation affinity for desired compounds, thermal properties, and physical properties such as density and viscosity. SCFs can be modified by changing temperature or pressure to attain transport or solvation properties that are more like a gas or a liquid, respectively. IL enhanced SCF extraction utilizes these properties to create a separation technique that may be able to selectively separate a mixture into its base compounds. The current project is to demonstrate this separation technique by utilizing the Peng-Robinson Equation of State with Van der Waals mixing rules to model the solubility of different dyes in the SCCO 2 to determine the pressure needed to ensure the maximum amount of solubility within reason. Preliminary experiments have been conducted to transfer dye from a solid mixture to an IL and from a dye-saturated IL to a pure IL. All experiments conducted have supported the hypothesis that SCFs can be used to as a pathway to transport compounds from solid/liquid to another IL. A computer program, COSMO-RS, has been utilized as a screening method to analyze ILs and various dyes to calculate the activity coefficients of the ionic liquid. This allows a partition coefficient to be calculated and a combination of dye/IL to be selected to use in upcoming experiments. The current goal of the work is to selectively separate two different dyes into two different ILs, using disperse dyes as model compounds to demonstrate the utility of non-contact separation. The eventual goal, however, is to move from dyes to more practical implications such as extracting pharmaceutical compounds using this method, improving separation techniques in the chemical engineering industry.

title: Towards Fractionation of Soybean Meals in a Water- and Chemical-Free Environment
abstract: Traditional wet fractionation techniques have many drawbacks due to the utilization of acid, alkali and chemicals which cause denaturation and, consequently, loss of protein solubility. In addition, plenty amount of resources such as water and energy are required to produce protein isolates using wet methods. In contrast, dry separation processes such as air classification, sieving and tribo-electrostatic separation preserve native functionality of proteins. The aim of this research is to implement the novel tribo-electrostatic separation technique for the production of protein-rich and fiber-rich fractions from defatted soybean ( glycine max ) flour followed by optimizing the separation operating parameters. The tribo-electrostatic separation is based on the phenomena that proteins have better chargeability properties than carbohydrates. This can be explained by the presence of many ionizable groups in proteins such as amine groups, carboxyl groups and side chains. Our custom-built separation unit including a tribo-charging tube, separation chamber with two oppositely charged electrodes, and fluidized bed was implemented in the Bioprocess Engineering Research Laboratory at Howard University. In this study, soybean particles were first charged in the charging tube and then separated in the fractionation chamber based on the acquired charges under the influence of external electric field. The optimization of process parameters was performed. We tested two different air flow rates (7LPM and 15LPM) and three plate voltages (±1kV, ±3.5kV, and ±6.5kV). At the most optimal processes conditions, the initial protein and fiber contents of soybean flour were increased from 55.3% and 15.3% to 58.4% and 19.6%, respectively. These accounted for 66.5% of the total protein and 60.8% of the total fiber. This novel technology is water-free, chemical-free and eco-friendly alternative to the traditional wet protein separation methods.

title: Ionic Liquid Enhanced Supercritical Fluid Extraction
abstract: Ionic liquid enhanced supercritical fluid extraction (ILESCFE) is a novel, environmentally benign extraction process that carries the potential to be a widely applicable, tunable alternative to traditional extractions. Traditional extractions rely heavily on volatile organic solvents which are often toxic and can easily escape into the environment as fugitive emissions. ILESCFE eliminates the issue of fugitive emissions due to the fact that the supercritical fluid (SCF) is environmentally benign and ionic liquids (ILs) effectively lack a vapor pressure. The properties of the SCF can be tuned by slight adjustments to temperature and pressure and ILs can be tailored to specific tasks through the addition of different functional groups and by using different cation-anion pairs. ILESCFE operates under the 0 th Law of Thermodynamics to accomplish no-contact in situ concentration of the solute into the desired ionic liquid. Systems of multiple ionic liquids can be designed to achieve high selectivity of the desired solute in an extraction. This research focuses on modelling with COSMO-RS which is a quantum chemistry-based method that can predict the behavior (activity coefficients) of species in a mixture. COSMO-RS can be used to quickly screen countless ionic liquids to determine which ILs exhibit the proper selectivity for a given solute. Preliminary screening has indicated efficacy of COSMO-RS for the scope of this project. Qualitative proof-of-concept experiments have been performed in a Parr bomb reactor at 40 °C and 1450 psi with various hold times. Solid Disperse Orange 1 has been successfully concentrated in situ to a generic IL (1-hexyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(triflouromethylsulfonyl)imide). The transfer of Disperse Orange 1 saturated in a generic ionic liquid to the same pure ionic liquid has also been successfully demonstrated in a proof of concept experiment. These experiments demonstrated transfer of a solute from both its pure solid form and saturated in a liquid. Selectivity has been demonstrated as well through the in situ concentration of a solid mixture of Disperse Orange 1 and Methylene Blue to a generic IL with the end result showing a higher affinity for Disperse Orange 1. Dyes have been used as model compounds due to the ease in which quantitative measurements can be taken through the use of UV-Vis spectroscopy.

title: Residence Time Distribution and Holdup in Centrifugal Extractors
abstract: Annular centrifugal extractors (ACE) are liquid-liquid extractors which achieve high extractive efficiencies with a fast residence time. However, due to a fundamental lack of understanding of the driving force and the kinetics of ACE units, scale-up is, currently, not feasible. This study seeks to quantitatively understand the hydrodynamics of the ACE units through phase holdups and residence time distributions (RTD). Ultimately, data from this study will help build mathematical models to improve the physical description of the system. To experimentally determine RTD and holdup, organic (30% tributyl phosphate in isopar) and aqueous (0.0071% nitric acid solution) streams were brought to steady-state through a 4-pack extractor unit. Then, Sudan I dye was added to the inlet organic stream, and concentration data was collected over a 10-minute period from the organic outlet stream. Subsequently, RTD and holdup were quantitatively calculated with the concentration data.

topic: 174cc- Monoethanolamine Based DES for CO 2 Absorption: Insights from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
title: Monoethanolamine Based DES for CO 2 Absorption: Insights from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
abstract: Several ionic liquids have been designed to absorb CO 2 and thereby decrease greenhouse gas emissions. Among them, novel deep eutectic solvents (DESs), with their commercially attractive properties, have recently been studied for CO 2 capture process. In our previous work we have studied molecular structure of DESs composed methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide (MTPPBr) and mono ethanol amine (MEA) at molar ratio 1:6, 1:7 and 1:8, which are known to have high CO 2 absorption capacity. In current work, we analyze interactions between above mentioned DESs and CO 2 using molecular dynamics simulations to understand CO 2 absorption process. Results based on interaction energy and radial distribution functions (rdfs) have shown strong interactions between MEA/Br and CO 2 suggesting the capture of CO 2 by these compounds. Additionally, low diffusion coefficients of ions suggest high viscosity of DESs, an impediment to its commercial development. Water was added to DESs in different amount, to analyze the influence of water on to DESs’ viscosity. Results show that structure of DESs remains same up to 50% of water in DESs, while viscosity of DESs starts to decrease significantly above 50%. For same purpose, DESs were also examined at higher temperature that lead to significant decrease of viscosity. Taken together, work assists in understanding interactions between CO 2 and DESs’ component and CO 2 absorption mechanism, additionally it suggests methods to decrease DESs viscosity, along with optimized process conditions, for further industrial implementation.

topic: 174bc- PAT-Facilitated Crystallization Development and Particle Engineering Via Mechanistic Understanding
title: PAT-Facilitated Crystallization Development and Particle Engineering Via Mechanistic Understanding
abstract: A development compound X which has a salt-formation step with a carboxylic acid was investigated to enhance understanding of its crystallization process. PAT Raman and FBRM were used to monitor the form transformation in real time and both were found to be indicative of the crystallization kinetics. A mechanistic model for solid form transformation was proposed based on the sequence of events involved and the mechanism was verified by the kinetic profiles revealed by Raman. A number of process variables were studied in a design of experiment (DoE) setting in order to identify the factors that impact the final attributes of the product such as particle size and morphology. The investigation, specifically through the precise quantitation by PAT, indicated the crystallization is primarily dictated by solvent composition and temperature. Other process variables such as seeds characteristics and acid addition rate were also evaluated and their effects on the outcome were found to be secondary. This insight helped steer the focus of development efforts to enhance the robustness of the process. A quantitative prediction model on particle size was extracted from the array of experiments and its accuracy was demonstrated at various spots of the parameter range covered by the study.

topic: 174by- Wnt-Notch Signaling Interactions during Neural and Glial Patterning of Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
title: Wnt-Notch Signaling Interactions during Neural and Glial Patterning of Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
abstract: Wnt-Notch Signaling Interactions during Neural and Glial Patterning of Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells Julie Bejoy 1 , Brent Bijonowski 1 , Teng Ma 1 , Yan Li 1,2 1 Department of Chemical and Biomedical Engineering; FAMU-FSU College of Engineering; Florida State University; Tallahassee, FL USA 2 Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, Florida State University, Tallahassee, Florida, USA Introduction: The human brain formation involves complicated processing which is regulated by a gene regulatory network involving different signaling pathways. The cross-regulatory interactions between elements of different pathways affect the process of cell fate assignment during neural and glial tissue patterning. In this study, the interactions between Wnt and Notch pathways, the two major pathways that influence neural and glial differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) individually, were investigated. In particular, the synergistic effects of Wnt-Notch pathway on the neural patterning processes along anterior-posterior (A-P) or dorsal-ventral (D-V) axis of hiPSC-derived cortical spheroids were explored. The human cortical spheroids derived from hiPSCs were treated with Wnt activator CHIR99021 (CHIR), Wnt inhibitor IWP4, Notch inhibitor (DAPT) individually, or in combinations (CHIR+DAPT, IWP4+DAPT). Materials and Methods: Human iPSK3 cells were seeded into Ultra-Low Attachment (ULA) 24-well plates. The formed EBs were treated with dual SMAD signaling inhibitors 10 μM SB431542 and 100 nM LDN193189. After 8 days, the cells were treated with fibroblast growth factor-2 and retinoic acid until day 16. During day 16-21, the spheroids were treated with six different conditions: (1) control, no small molecule was used; (2) CHIR99021 (10 μM), which activates Wnt signaling by inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase-3β; (3) IWP4, which inhibits Wnt signaling through the porcupine and thereby reducing the production of Wnt proteins; (4) the Notch inhibitor DAPT. The γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT can inhibit the γ-secretase dependent S3 cleavage of Notch, which releases the Notch internal cytoplasmic domain; (5) CHIR99021 plus DAPT (C+D); (6) IWP4 plus DAPT (I+D). To elucidate the influence of regional identity of neural progenitors on glial differentiation, the spheroids (day 21) of the six conditions were switched to BMP-4 treatment up to day 32. Results and Discussion: In our study, combinational treatments of Wnt and Notch modulators affected brain regional identity of iPSC-derived spheroids. The addition of DAPT to CHIR or IWP4 influences neural patterning effects of canonical Wnt pathway. Notch inhibition with DAPT reduced the hindbrain marker HOXB4, but the CHIR treatment was able to maintain HOXB4 expression in the presence of DAPT. Analysis of forebrain markers TBR1 and FOXG1 showed that IWP4 cannot maintain their expression in the presence of DAPT. I+D also reduced the expression of ventral forebrain marker Nkx2.1. The cortical spheroids that were treated with Wnt and Notch signaling modulators were then switched to gliogenesis by BMP4 treatment. The results showed that the CHIR group expressed the higher levels of astrocyte markers GFAP and Vimentin compared to the other groups. This might be because that CHIR treatment increased Notch activity and Notch ligand expression in the derived cortical spheroids. The lowest expression of astrocyte markers was shown in I+D group, indicating the dominance of DAPT treatment over IWP4 treatment on astrocyte differentiation and importance of Notch activation for astrogliogenesis. Conclusions: In this study, the functional cross-talk between Wnt and Notch signaling on neural and glial tissue patterning from hiPSCs were investigated using Wnt and Notch modulators. The results suggested the possibility of repressing effects of Notch inhibitor DAPT on Wnt inhibition and the positive impact of Wnt activation on Notch signaling for brain regional identity of hiPSC-derived cortical spheroids. Notch inhibition with DAPT reduced the hindbrain marker HOXB4, but CHIR was able to maintain HOXB4 expression in the presence of DAPT. Analysis of forebrain markers TBR1 and FOXG1 showed that IWP4 plus DAPT reduced forebrain marker expression. CHIR reduced the impact of DAPT on brain regional patterning whereas DAPT reduced Wnt inhibition effects. By switching the derived cortical spheroids to gliogenesis with BMP4, Wnt activator CHIR promoted the expression of astrocyte markers GFAP and Vimentin. The addition of Notch inhibitor DAPT to CHIR reduced astrocyte marker expression, confirming the importance of Notch activation on astrocyte generation. topic: 174br- Efficient Degradation of Imidacloprid through Biochar Activated Sodium Percarbonate
title: Efficient Degradation of Imidacloprid through Biochar Activated Sodium Percarbonate
abstract: Metal-free carbonaceous materials have been evaluated for the very first time to activate sodium percarbonate (SPC) for the degradation of insecticides. Palm empty fruit bunch biochar (PEFBB) was produced using pyrolyzation process. During this research work, a relatively low-cost carbonaceous material under limited oxygen supply for the activation of SPC to degrade imidacloprid was studied. The pyrolysis temperature was found to be a key parameter for the activation of SPC through biochar in the successive batch experiments. The degradation efficiency of imidacloprid considerably improved from 5.2 to 81.9 % when pyrolysis temperature increased from 250-850 o C. The degradation efficiency in the imidacloprid contaminated tap and ground water was 73.4 and 59.8% respectively. The elimination of excessive oxygen functional groups of biochar was found due to its higher temperatures, producing more defect structures with possible transformation and modulation of sp 3 carbons, thus enhancing the activation potential of biochar towards SPC. In addition, three intermediate products were identified and two different pathways were proposed as the major imidacloprid degradation. The reactive oxygen species (ROS) were studied using radical scavengers and electron spin resonance (ESR) to verify the dominant generation of hydroxyl radicals (OH ● ) in the biochar/SPC system. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR), Raman analysis and ESR combined X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) elucidated the generation of OH ● as well as superoxide (O 2 ●– ) free radicals due to the biochar defect structure. In conclusion, biochar activated SPC process is promising technique for the imidacloprid degradation that significantly enhance its application in the imidacloprid contaminated sites.

topic: 174ai- Crude Oil Spot Sampling Methods and Their Impact on Thermophysical Properties
title: Crude Oil Spot Sampling Methods and Their Impact on Thermophysical Properties
abstract: In many situations, spot sampling provides an economic means by which aliquots of crude oil can be captured from various points in the supply chain for composition, bubble point pressure, density, and sulfur content property analysis. However, inadvertent introduction of N 2 and other gases in sample handling systems during the sampling, transport, and analysis steps can cause difficulties when trying to assess the properties of the parent materials. These difficulties were investigated when compositions of crudes were measured via several analytical methods (ASTM D7169, ASTM D7900, ASTM D8003, GPA 2103, GPA 2177, GOR) on samples obtained from supply chains in North Dakota and Texas using a variety of spot sampling methods/containers (ASTM D3700, GPA 2174, ASTM D8009, ASTM 4057). The N 2 contents were compared to whole oil compositions derived from a tight-line flash gas compositional analysis paired with an Equation of State (EOS) model. The tight-line system was configured so that the pre-conditioning system and analytical equipment were connected directly to the oil process piping in the field. This minimized sample handling and potential for introducing air, and furthermore provided excess volume of oil to purge the pre-conditioning and analytical equipment with parent material. The whole oil compositions resulting from both the spot sampling and tight-line sample collection methods were used as input to a commercially available process simulator to calculate thermophysical properties. The prevalence of N 2 in the spot samples significantly changed calculated thermophysical properties, which can impact process models and classification of materials for transportation. The Crude Oil Characterization Research Study (funded by US DOE, DOT, and Transport Canada: http://energy.gov/fe/articles/crude-oil-characteristics-research , https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2018/02/the-great-crude-oil-fireball-test/552029/ ), seeks to understand the crude oil property differences between conventionally produced and tight oils. Recent activities analyzed the effects of sampling containers/techniques (ASTM D3700, GPA 2174, ASTM D8009, ASTM 4057) and sampling locations (Texas vs. North Dakota) on crude oil thermophysical property measurements. Different compositional measurement techniques (GPA 2103, GPA 2177, ASTM D7900, ASTM D7169, ASTM D8003, GOR flash) have been used to calculate these properties as well, providing insight into the features and limitations of these commercially available methodologies.
